title: Photocatalytic removal of textile wastewater-originated methylene blue and malachite green dyes using spent black tea ex

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The SBT-AgNP peak at 40.8° is assigned to the (200) plane, but for FCC silver (JCPDS 04-0783) the (200) reflection occurs at about 44.3°, not 40.8°. Likewise the chemically synthesized AgNP peak at 81.5° is assigned to (311), whereas Ag (311) is expected at about 77.4°; 81.5° is closer to (222).

predicted_errors.error_location: Optimization of parameters for AgNPs synthesis
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states '1 ml of varying concentration... AgNO3 salt was added to the 9 ml of the prepared extract,' but the stated and later used ratios are biomass-to-salt ratios of 1:9, 2:8, etc. Adding 1 ml salt to 9 ml extract would give a 9:1 extract:salt ratio, contradicting the initial synthesis procedure ('1 ml of spent black tea extracts in 9 ml of (100 mM) AgNO3').
The paper reports 'zeta deviation of 10.8 and -13.7 mV.' A deviation/standard deviation cannot be negative; -13.7 mV appears to be a zeta-potential value rather than a deviation.

It states that 100 mM AgNO3 showed the highest absorption signal (2.8), then concludes that 50 mM was efficient because it 'gave comparatively more absorption signals' than 100 mM, although the 50 mM peak was lower (2.35) and the difference is stated as 0.45 OD points.

predicted_errors.error_location: UV-Vis characterization of chemically synthesized AgNPs
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says the chemically synthesized AgNPs showed their 'characteristic peak at 310 nm.' For citrate-reduced AgNPs with an average size around 114 nm, the silver surface plasmon resonance should be near 400-450 nm, consistent with the SBT-AgNP peak at about 423 nm. A 310 nm peak is not characteristic of these Ag nanoparticles.

predicted_errors.error_location: SEM results / paragraph following particle-size discussion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'The presence of clear zone indicates the inhibition of bacterial growth by nanoparticles' and that the samples 'show different antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.' No antibacterial experiment or clearing-zone assay is described anywhere in the methods or results, so these claims are unsupported.

The paper claims 'SBT-AgNPs exhibit superior stability over various other waste materials, including green tea and coffee,' but no comparative stability data or referenced comparative study is provided to support this claim.
